You know, it's like something one of Zidane's coaches once said. If you don't know what to do with the ball, give it to Zidane. He'll figure it out, so... You see, that's the thing. It's a quality not every player has. You're taking the ball. You're taking responsibility. You're taking the initiative. You are not afraid to fail. You're not afraid to make a mistake. Cristiano had a moment like that. He missed a penalty, and later in the same match, he stepped up to take another one. Think about that. You take the first penalty. You miss it. Then another penalty comes along, and you still step up to take it. Because if you miss two penalties in the same game, you're under a lot of pressure, right? But that's the point. You're not afraid to fail. As a leader, you take the initiative, and you're you're willing to take risks. That's honestly the beauty of it, the beauty of sports in general. The bigger the risk, the bigger the potential for greatness. If there's no risk, then there's no... You can't make, can't put yourself in the category of athletes people will talk about as some of the best ever. - Especially when it's a high-level game like the World Cup and... - Yes. The more risk, the sweeter the victory. There must be risk. - That's why they often speak of Maradona as a great player. There are many great players. He's great- - One of them, yeah - ...for many reasons. But one reason is that he kinda, kinda carried the team on his shoulders. - He took the initiative and carried them. That's, that's when he led Napoli, you know? When he led Napoli to the league title. Who knew Napoli then? Maradona came from Barcelona to Napoli and made them champions, and the whole stadium was named after him. Many guys played in Napoli, but there was never anyone like Maradona. And recently, I saw somewhere, or I think someone pointed out, the pressure on the guys who are transferring to Napoli. Whoever you are, you will always be in Maradona's shadow, and you stay in the shadow because fans will never give you the credit you might deserve because they will always compare you to him. Are you Maradona or not? And if you're not Maradona, you will never get full recognition. - I want to say that one of the things that makes Messi great, I think, is that he really had to live in such a shadow of Maradona, and especially with the World Cup. - Yes. - It's not easy. - And he came out of it. - Hard to emerge from that shadow. - Yes. And he won the World Cup, yeah. In that sense, you have to give Messi his due. I'm addressing the Real Madrid fans now. Ours, yours, both sides. - You're explaining it to them. - Yeah, yeah. - I got you. - Most of them, I think even if they don't like Barcelona, they still recognize Messi's greatness. - I know that you met Zlatan. You talked to him. I think he's one of the most, most self-confident people in football, in the world in general. What do you think about this confidence? Of course, he's joking around a little bit, but I think he really believes in himself. - Well, yeah, he does. He does. I've known Zlatan for years now. We get along well, and I know his kids, and I like his personality. I like his confidence. I mean, he's a unique player. There are not many Zlatans in football. You know, wherever he played, he always scored. He's a goal scorer. He is that kind of center forward, and he always carried the team. He was a leader wherever he transferred. It doesn't matter. Milan, Inter, Juventus, when he moved to LA Galaxy or Paris Saint-Germain. He was a leader everywhere he went, with the national team, with his clubs. He was always the guy driving the team forward, taking the initiative. And honestly, he cemented his place as one of the greatest players to ever play the game. And yeah, maybe he was... When it comes to trophies, not individual achievements, but team honors, Sweden wasn't such a Wasn't exactly the greatest team, and some of the clubs he played for didn't always win the biggest trophies. But as an athlete, as an individual, as a person, he is a very strong athlete. - We talked a lot about Dagestan, talked a lot about America. You're in Dubai a lot these days. Do you like it there? Also, you have spoken very highly about Sheikh Hamdan. What do you like about Dubai? What do you like about this region? And what do you respect about Sheikh Hamdan? - Our team's been in Dubai for seven to eight years now. We train at the Nad Al Sheba Sports Complex. The NAS Sports Complex, this is under Sheikh Hamdan's office. It's like his home, his place. We train there, we eat there, we live there. Sheikh Hamdan helps us with everything and takes care of us. The way he treats us, what he does for us, his support is just limitless. He supports us in everything, and it's not just one, two, or three years. It's already been seven or eight years. And I am very, very grateful to him. The way he welcomed us, took us in, and helped us, continues to help, it's hard to put it into words how grateful we are. Our entire team is very grateful to him, and he knows it. So in general, Dubai has become... Actually, the Emirates, Dubai, and Abu Dhabi have become like a second home for us. And so it happened that over the last six or seven years, the UFC has been holding events in Abu Dhabi, and the PFL has been putting on events in Dubai. These are two of the biggest MMA organizations in the world, and a lot of our guys compete there. We arrive before the fight, we stay, we do training camps, they compete. We are incredibly fortunate that we have support at the government level. In Abu Dhabi, we've been supported by Sheikh Mohammed, Sheikh Tahnoon, and Sheikh Mansour. And in Dubai, Sheikh Hamdan has really taken us in like his own team, like younger brothers. In that respect, we've been incredibly fortunate, and our entire team is deeply grateful for their support. - And they've created a country that has become one of the world's central hubs. People from everywhere travel there. - It's unique, right? The local population is only around one and a half million people, actually even less than that. But, you know, there's such an influx of tourists, people, business people, major events, and everything happening in terms of business and sports is just incredible. What's happening in Dubai and Abu Dhabi is, it's like nothing else. The only places you could really compare it to are major global cities like New York, London, Paris, Tokyo. But those are huge metropolitan areas with populations of well over twenty million people, and they have centuries of history behind them. And here, they've built cities, an entire country really, in just a few decades and turned it into a kind of magnet. It's like a magnet that attracts everyone. The country's location, its logistics, the sheer number of people coming in, not just visiting, but wanting to move there, live there, and start businesses, it's remarkable. It's a unique place in today's world. With everything that's happening around the globe right now, this country really stands out because of the opportunities it offers. It's unique in that sense. - Now I'd like to ask you this. For you, your Muslim faith and God, it's obviously central to your life and to who you are. Can you explain what role God plays in your life? - Well, first of all, I was born, raised, and brought up in a Muslim family, in a Muslim community. Since childhood, religion's always been the most important thing for me. And when I say religion, the first thing I mean is Salah, Namaz. And my entire life in general, my daily routine, the way I lived, trained, studied, and everything else has always been built around Salah. The rest was scheduled around it. Even today, when I was choosing time for this podcast, I knew we'd be talking for a couple of hours, so I deliberately picked a time right after the midday prayer. I pray, come here, finish up here with you, and then go pray again. That's how my life's been, and still is, and that's how it will continue to be, I hope. I've always tried to organize my life around worship, because first and foremost, my purpose in this life is to worship the one God. Everything that happens after that is, it's secondary, so to speak. And faith in God and learning more and just striving to get closer to God, that continues throughout our entire lives. So in that regard, I'm very grateful to the Almighty for opening this door of understanding and reflection for me, for helping me realize that we are all servants of God and that our purpose in life is to serve one God. - And as you were explaining that helped you in your career in the sense that, you know, psychologically, by keeping you from letting success go to your head? - That helped me with everything. I've always placed my only hope in the Almighty. Whatever situation I might face, I've always believed that only the Almighty can truly make it easier for me. And when it comes to not letting success go to your head, not becoming proud, not becoming full of yourself, religion and my faith in Allah have helped me with that too. I truly believe that only faith can help a person get through life's hardest trials. And sometimes I think about people who suffer the loss of a loved one, someone very close to them. For example, when I lost my father, I remember thinking to myself, "If I didn't believe in the Almighty, if I didn't have faith in God and understand that it was predestined, that we all come into this world and then leave it, that no one stays here forever, that no one belongs to anyone, and we all belong to the Almighty, and that we will all return to Him, I don't know how I would have coped with it." I'm a very emotional person. I think it would have been extremely difficult for me to go through all of that without faith. In that sense, I feel fortunate to have this understanding. - So faith really helped you when you lost your father? - This was the only thing that helped. Nothing else worked. I know a couple of people who have lost someone very close to them, and they struggle to accept it. They would ask, "Why? Why? Why?" So many questions. I told them, to answer that question, you need to go deeper into religion and try to understand why were you even born in the first place, and why do these thoughts even come into your head? And what if you didn't have any thoughts at all? What if you couldn't think, couldn't understand anything? These thoughts, this awareness, your mind, your abilities, none of that was there before. Then it appeared. Why? That's the question. None of us existed. Then we were born. We were little. We weren't aware of anything. We didn't remember anything. Then little by little, we grew up and became adults. We became successful, became somebody. We became who we are. So why did all of this come specifically to you? There are so many questions like that. And so these questions are, let's say, a kind of guide through life. And for me that's what religion is. It guides me and helps me. - You often say, "Alhamdulillah, all praise to God." That's very powerful, that sense of gratitude. Can you tell us, can you explain why you say it so often? - You know the saying, the tongue speaks what the heart is full of. The way you speak shows what's in your heart. If you have something dark in your heart, your words will show it, no doubt. We all have some dark parts in our hearts. Every single person has them. Sometimes they come out in what we say, how we express ourselves, what we share with people, and so on. Everyone has that. But if your heart is mostly good and pure, then that will also be reflected in your speech. And And I just like praising the Almighty and giving all the credit for my success back to Him because everything we have is given to us by the Almighty. Throughout the history, there have been many people who made big mistakes after becoming successful, powerful, and wealthy, and they started saying, "No, no, this happened to me because I'm so great, because I'm so, I'm so intelligent, because I had vision, because I've got the brains, because I'm extremely capable. That's why all of this came my way." But at the same time, there were many others who worked just as hard, who weren't any less intelligent, and the Almighty just didn't give it to them. He chose you and gave it to you, and you just have to give the credit back to Him. You shouldn't take the credit for yourself. That's what I believe. And it's something I've come to through studying my religion. I understand that everything the Almighty has given to me is not because of who I am. It's simply something God has given me as a test to test me and, in the end, see which of my deeds outweigh the others, the good or the bad. Because as a believer, I believe that there will be judgment and everything we have, everything we do, every action we take, we will be held accountable for it. There will be a day of judgment, there will be scales, and everything will be weighed. - What advice would you give young people about life and their careers? Millions of people are watching you and deeply respect you. What would you say about how to live your life? And how do you find your path and stay on it? - Well, I wouldn't want to speak just from my own perspective. I'd rather bring people back to the scripture, to what the Almighty said, "Read." That's the first word revealed in the Holy Quran. The first command is read or ikra. So to everyone listening to or watching this podcast, I would want to bring them back to that. Read, meaning what? Educate yourself, observe, learn, improve, but don't stay in one place. And anything a person is truly looking for, if they genuinely want to find it, not just find an answer, but find the truth, they can reach it, but they can never reach it without reading. They need to read. When a person reads, what they read enters them into their body, their heart, their mind, and it triggers a search. A search for knowledge begins inside them, but if you don't read, you won't find anything. Just listening to someone is one thing, but reading is something different. So my advice would be read and find within yourself the strength to come closer to one God and seek to understand why we were sent here in the first place. Today, you and me, we're almost the same age. So let's just think about this. For example, my grandfather on my mother's side passed away in two thousand and three. Now it's twenty twenty-six. He's been lying in the grave for twenty-three years. And then there was his grandfather, or let's say his great-grandfather who also died and has been in the grave for over a hundred years, roughly speaking. But what about people who died two thousand years ago? They've been in the grave for two thousand years. What's next? It's a good question, isn't it? They've just been in the grave all this time, and that's it. So what was the purpose of their life? A person has been in the grave for two thousand years, but maybe lived for seventy years. Roughly speaking, let's say one hundred. They lived for one hundred years and have been in the grave for two thousand. So what matters more, those one hundred years or these two thousand years? And what happens after those two thousand years end? People believe different things, whether there is a day of judgment or not. That's where the difference lies between a believer and a non-believer. After everyone is resurrected, there will be the day of judgment. There will be judgment, and after that, people will enter eternity. Eternity compared to eternity, what are two thousand years? They're nothing. And we live for, let's say, seventy years. And many people choose those seventy years over eternal life. And if a person understands that these seventy years they have here, roughly speaking, seventy or eighty years are meant to be used to prepare for what comes after, so that when the day of judgment arrives, and after that judgment they can live forever, not in hell, but in heaven. If that becomes their ultimate goal, then they will strive to do good deeds because they will fear the day of judgment. And that's really what life is about, preparing yourself for the day of judgment. - That's true. To truly understand life and its deeper meaning, you have to think about eternity. Only then can you really understand your role. - Actually, it can keep a person away from evil. From evil and, and it can stop them from treating other people badly. It can hold a person back. But if you don't have that understanding, if a person lives completely convinced that there's nothing after death, what's there to stop him from doing evil? Just like that. What do you think? And on top of that, an even more dangerous combination. You become powerful, wealthy, and you become famous. What now? Suddenly every door is open to you. Just imagine a person like that. And on top of all that, he doesn't believe in the day of judgment. He doesn't believe he'll be held accountable for his actions. That's, you know, it's like a nuclear bomb. He can end up causing harm to people everywhere. But if you know that for everything you have here, you'll eventually have to answer, that there will be a day of judgment and that you'll be called to account, and if you fail that test, you'll burn in hell forever. That'll make you rein yourself in a little. You'll have to take that into consideration. You'll have to tighten things up a little. You'll begin to understand that you're not nearly as important as the image you've created of yourself in your own mind. You start becoming more, as Americans say, down to earth. You become more grounded. You're not flying, you're walking on the ground. - You once put it beautifully. You can allow money and fame to stay in your hand, but not in your heart. You've still got many years ahead of you, but you're already an example of someone who's become famous, made money, and remained the same person. - If money stays in your hands and not in your heart That's a good thing. But the moment it gets into a person's heart, it corrupts them. Once it's there, it's very difficult to pull it out of your heart. If you have wealth in your hands and use it properly for good causes, for the right purposes, for people in need, for your family, relatives, friends, people from your hometown, that's a good thing. But as soon as that wealth gets into your heart, it becomes very difficult to share it with others. And this is a very dangerous place for a person to end up. And I'm sorry, but as a believer, I believe that most people in hell will be wealthy. - One of the reasons millions of people find you so interesting to watch is that you're constantly growing. First, you were a great fighter. Now you're becoming a leader. Your wisdom just keeps increasing. You're evolving as a person, but still the core values remain. It's good to see, inspiring for people. Money and fame haven't changed you. You're just growing as a human being, as you always have. - I hope it's in the right direction. It's just, the thing is people only see the good. They don't see the bad. And we all have the good side and the bad side. Everyone, sadly. And especially when it comes to celebrities, we only show the best side of ourselves. Even when you post photos, you only post the good ones, the pictures where you look your best. So I hope that the way people see me, as you pointed out, is the way I really am, because it's difficult to judge yourself objectively. You're always biased when it comes to yourself. That's how it is. We tend to think highly of ourselves, right? You can't really see yourself objectively. We hide our flaws and put our best qualities on display. Sometimes people even start believing in a fake version of themselves. For me, I try to stay on the honest path throughout my life to remain true to who I really am and to show my true self to people. Maybe not everyone agrees with my behavior, my opinions, my worldview, or my attitudes toward, towards sports, religion, and other things. Not everyone shares my views. Not everyone is a fan of mine. There are people who, let's say, see me very differently. So I'm just... I've tried, I continue to try to be who I am. That's all. And I hope that my ending will be a good one, too. Well, you know, at least that's my hope. - You've stayed the same, but you've also grown. I mean, today you even managed to say something nice about Barça. So see, that's progress. Yeah. Well done. - Come on, without Barcelona, there wouldn't be Real Madrid. If the Spanish league didn't have either Real Madrid or Barcelona, it just wouldn't be the same. They've been competing against each other for how many years? One hundred twenty. It's hard to imagine Barcelona and Real Madrid without each other, and so is the Spanish league without that rivalry. It's impossible to imagine. So yeah, we have to give you some credit, but Real Madrid is the royal club. Come on. It's the best. You know? - And thanks to both of them, we've been able to enjoy truly incredible football for so many years. - For so many years, yeah. - Um, Khabib, brother, I don't even have the words to explain how honored I am that you're here talking with me today and showing me so much warmth. There's no way to fully express what you mean to millions of your fans around the world, including me. Thank you so much for everything. Thank you for this conversation. - Thank you. Thank you very much, Lex. - Thank you for listening to this conversation with Khabib Nurmagomedov. And again, thank you for everything. I love you all. Goodbye, my friends. See you next time.

items.title: Gary Gallagher: American Civil War, Slavery, Lincoln, Grant & Lee | Lex Fridman Podcast #499
items.transcript_text:
- You cannot control what a great military event can set loose. More battle casualties than US forces had suffered in every war combined down to that point happened in two days. Two and a half months after that, George B. McClellan's army engaged with Lee's army in what came to be called the Seven Days Battles at Richmond, 36,000 casualties. So those two together just showed that this was gonna be on a totally different scale. He added a psychological twist. What, what Grant envisioned his doing, and Sheridan actually did it in the Shenandoah Valley before Sherman did it in Georgia, is go into an agriculturally productive area, burn the mills, kill the livestock, destroy the crops, lay waste to it so that it can't be a logistical support of the Confederacy anymore. Sheridan did it in the Shenandoah Valley, and then Sherman did it in Georgia. But Sherman said, "But I'm also going to break them psychologically. I'm gonna show them that my army can go wherever it wants to go whenever it wants to go, and there's nothing Jefferson Davis can do about it." The great forces are all that matters and individuals don't really matter notion of history I think is ridiculous. Individuals really matter. For the United States, Lincoln and Grant matter beyond calculation- ... in this war. And on the Confederate side, if you take Lee out of the picture, the war doesn't last nearly as long as it does. In terms of causation, if you take slavery out of the picture, there is no Civil War, period. - The following is a conversation with Gary Gallagher, a historian of the American Civil War. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. To support it, please check out our sponsors in the description where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. And now, dear friends, here's Gary Gallagher. The American Civil War broke out in 1861. What were the causes of the Civil War? Could it have been avoided, or was it inevitable? - I don't know if anything is inevitable in history, but it's certainly safe to say that the conditions were in place to make it possible- ... by the winter of 1860, '61, and the conditions that made it possible were all related to the institution of slavery and its effects both in the states where slavery was allowed and the states where it was not allowed. And there had been a series of tensions that grew in the decade preceding the 1850s. It's not that one side wants to get rid of slavery and the other side wants to protect slavery. I'm talking about the white people in the United States now who would be making the political decisions. It's a question of whether slavery was going to be able to expand into federal territories. That is what really created the starkest difference between the two sections in the 1850s, even in the late 1840s. The issues that came to most, uh, perilous a point in the view of many people then had to do with whether slavery would be allowed only where it already existed, or would it be allowed to expand. If it could expand, then it seemed that it might be conceivable at some point even that the slaveholding states could end up with a majority. They were in a minority by 1860, '61 and feeling beleaguered, feeling threatened. They'd long since lost the population race to the free states. Early in the nation, the most powerful states were slaveholding states. Virginia was by far the most important state. Four of the first five presidents were from Virginia, all slaveholders, all prominent members of the slaveholding class. Those days were long gone by the late 1850s. - So that's an important thing to say. It wasn't before the Civil War a discussion about abolishing slavery. It's about whether slavery, the institution of slavery should be expanded. - Allowed to expand into federal territories. There, there is a portion of the white population that is adamantly in favor of getting rid of slavery immediately. The abolitionists, they... There was even a political party called the Liberty Party, that ran a candidate in 1840 and they got a handful of thousand votes. They reached their high point in 1844. They got about two and a half percent of the vote. The abolitionists are a tiny minority among the— even in the North, tiny minority among the white people of the United States. The African American population, nearly four million of them by 1860, of course, would have embraced it instantly and yearned for it. But in the white population, the abolitionists are a tiny minority. They are much despised even across much of the North because they were seen as agitators who roiled the Union and deepened rifts that might bring a significant political break. - So how did this escalate to a civil war, this almost policy discussion about the institution of slavery? How did it actually escalate? - It escalated into a civil war because in the presidential election of 1860... There'd been two party systems in the United States. The first party system, the Republicans, the Jeffersonian Republicans versus the Federalists. After that, there was, the two parties were the Whig Party against the Democratic Party. The Democratic Party grew out of the Jeffersonian Republican Party. It's the same party. The Whig Party foundered to a significant degree on the issue of slavery. How do you maintain a national party that has a wing in the Southern states and has a wing in the Northern free states that can handle the issue of slavery? The Democrats managed to do that. The Whigs could not do it, and so the Whig Party ran their last candidate in 1852, presidential candidate, significant candidate. And the Republican Party emerged in the mid-1850s, took most of the old Whigs into the Republican ranks and one of the Republican, the key Republican platform plank was no expansion of slavery into the territories. Not abolish slavery, no expansion. That was the key in 1856 when they ran their first candidate. In 1860, that is again the key plank in the Republican platform. The Republican platform in 1860 says where slavery exists it will continue, but it cannot expand into the territories. When white Southerners saw that, that meant that they were doomed to become an increasingly minority section in the nation, and you would have a federal government increasingly dominated by the free states that could then do the one thing that the white South could not countenance, and that is tamper with the institution of slavery in the South. The presidential election of 1860 brought the destruction of the last national party, which was the Democrats. They couldn't even settle on a candidate, so you end up with a Northern Democratic candidate running, Stephen A. Douglas, and a Southern candidate running. The convention fractured and John C. Breckinridge ran on the, on the Southern Democrat platform. You had a Unionist candidate running who just didn't wanna talk about slavery, let's talk about the Union, and you had Lincoln running as a Republican. When Lincoln won, the white South looked at Lincoln winning. Here's a guy who has said that he doesn't think slavery would expand, but he'd said more than that. He scared the white South more because in 1858, both Lincoln and William Henry Seward, these are two prominent, prominent Republicans, had said basically in separate speeches, the House Divided Speech on Lincoln's part, the Irrepressible Conflict Speech on Seward's part, that the nation could not continue in the long term half slave and half free. And everybody in the South knew which way they wanted it to be. They would want it to be no slavery. And so Lincoln's election scared the white South enough so that seven of the 15 slave-holding states seceded in response to Lincoln's election. They seceded between December 20th, when South Carolina went out, and the end of February. You had the deep South went out. - What was the general view amongst the populace towards slavery? Let's kind of lay it out. Let's you know, for the audience looking back, let's put ourselves in the mind space of how people saw the world, how people saw slavery, how people saw African Americans. - Well, the baseline among the white Americans, there were about 31, shade more than 31 million Americans in 1860 for the census of 1860. About four million of them were African Americans, three and a half million of those enslaved in the South. Anyway, among the white population, the average attitude toward Black people is what we would call profoundly prejudiced. Doesn't matter whether you... A lot of people think this is a Southern white thing. They're the only ones who were prejudiced. By our standards, the overwhelming majority of people in the free states were also deeply prejudiced. It's important to keep in mind that attitudes towards slavery and attitudes toward race do not, they're not necessarily the same. I mean, you could be against slavery and still be prejudiced against Black people. By our standards, many abolitionists were prejudiced against Black people. They... But the overwhelming majority of the white North, in the North, often had a hard time getting my students to understand the demographics in 1860. The free states in 1860 were more than 98% white. 98% white. African Americans are a tiny minority in the free states. Black people lived in the 15 slaveholding states in 1860. Most of the white North, by our standards, was very prejudiced. They were against the expansion of slavery into the territories because they thought that would circumscribe white opportunities to make an economic life in these federal territories, and they didn't want that to happen. About 45% of the people who lived in the free states were Democrats. Most Democrats had no problem with slavery. I mean, absolutely no problem with the institution of slavery. There would be more problems among Republicans, especially with extension of slavery, although many Democrats, white Democrats in the North were against that as well. The white South was overwhelmingly in favor of slavery. You often read the argument, the kind of neo-Confederate argument that they'll talk about how most Confederate soldiers didn't own slaves. That's true. The a large majority of families in the South did not own a single slave. But all white Southerners had a stake in slavery. They had a stake in it as a form of labor control, but more important than that, they had a stake in it as a means of social control. They knew, no matter what they said later in the Jim Crow era of how happy Black people were in the institution of slavery, they knew that Black people, of course, did not want to be enslaved, and they were afraid of what would happen if they weren't enslaved anymore. They had in the backs of their minds Haiti. Is that what's gonna... If you live in one of the coastal districts of South Carolina where 90% of the residents are enslaved and you're a white person, you probably don't sleep all that soundly at night if you think there's any chance that the Black people are not gonna remain under the control of the white people. So all white people in the South had a stake in slavery, not just some. All of them did, and there were all kinds of ways that it would go back and forth. If you were a modest farmer and grew a little bit of cotton, you didn't have your own cotton gin, you... but your more wealthy neighbor had a gin, could gin your cotton there, and then you would take your turn on the slave patrol, the slave patrols. So there's a reciprocity in that regard. - This is perhaps a bit outside the scope of what we'll talk about today, but just to lay out the context on slavery in general in human history, we should say that slavery was ubiquitous. It existed in virtually every major civilization in the history of humans. Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, China, the Islamic world, Africa, the Americas, North and South America. We should also say something that, as I was looking into this, another big topic, which is the Atlantic slave trade. He, he did everything that you should do to get an army in shape, and then he started a campaign. His plan, Lee was still at Fredericksburg. He was gonna get around Lee's left flank, come in behind him, force Lee to either retreat to Richmond or fight him on unfavorable ground. Everything went well with Hooker. He got going in late April until the moment of truth came. The moment of truth came on May 1st, 1863, when Lee, instead of retreating, left part of his army to watch one part of Hooker's and turned around to meet Hooker head-on near a crossroads called Chancellorsville a few miles west of Fredericksburg. And as soon as the fighting started, McClellan lost his nerve- ... pulled into a defensive position. And the upshot was after Lee and Jackson carried off a very successful flank attack, although it left Hooker still in a very strong position, Hooker in the end retreated, and it was another victory for Lee in a battle he never, ever should have won. He was outnumbered two to one, 135,000 to about 64,000. And when the moment of truth came, Joseph Hooker just lost his nerve. I mean, I really do believe that. I had fun working on this book. I wrote a ... A lot of books on campaigns are very long and detailed. I wanted a short book that would introduce interested readers who didn't really know that much perhaps to ... There's one of the maps. - So there are different, there's different positions, the different troops' positions. There's Hooker. - Yes. That is the ... The battle played out on May 1st, 2nd, and 3rd. There's the opening of the campaign. See the Rappahannock River, Fredericksburg. The armies are facing each other there. Hooker's plan was to leave part of his army to hold Lee's attention and move the rest up the river, up the Rappahannock, cross the Rappahannock and then the Rapidan, and get behind Lee so that Lee would be caught in a vise. He'd have Hooker in his rear and the anvil of other Union troops at Fredericksburg, and he thought that that would force Lee to retreat toward Richmond and that he could then harass him. They get around, they get behind Lee. They do exactly what Hooker wanted to do. He got to Chancellorsville. He had more than 70,000 men at Chancellorsville, and Lee doesn't find out till the very end of April what's going on, and then he decides to divide his army, leave 10,000 men to watch 40,000 Federals at Fredericksburg, and he and Stonewall Jackson head back toward Chancellorsville to meet Hooker. And they meet on May the 1st. The fighting starts on May the 1st. Everybody's upbeat in the Army of the Potomac. They've gotten around Lee's flank. They know they're behind him. Everything seems to go very well. Hooker said, "This is it. We've done it. We've done exactly what I wanted to do." And then the fighting starts the next day on May 1st. They march toward that place called Zoan Church. You can see there, it's just a little bit east of Chancellorsville. And the fighting, they collide about 11:00 in the morning. 2:00 that afternoon, Hooker orders a retreat. Everybody retreats back into this wilderness. It's a kind of cut-over, woodsy area, that it has very few roads, and he just hunkers down around Chancellorsville, hands the initiative to Lee. The next day, Jackson and Lee decide to send Jackson all the way around the right flank, and you see the flank march there. They come, they strike a Union corps that's exposed, commanded by a man named Oliver Otis Howard. Howard University is named after him. He headed the Freedmen's Bureau later in the war. They strike, they crush the 11th Corps, which has a very high German element in it, and there's a lot of ethnic prejudice that comes into play there by the other soldiers. But it ends up, the day ends up with Lee actually in worse shape than he was before. He's got two divisions over here under Anderson and McLaws on the lower right. He's not even in touch with Jackson's corps. Jackson was wounded that night by his own men, carried from the field. He'd die a few days later. And Hooker still, although Hooker is in between these two parts of Lee's army, he's in an ideal position. He's still just thinking about the defense even. Where on the morning of May 3rd, the two parts of Lee's army fight their way together around the Chancellorsville- ... clearing, and Hooker then retreats toward the north. You have this amazing moment on May the 3rd where Hooker, who's been stunned by an artillery round that hit a pillar he was leaning against at Chancellorsville- ... he had a concussion. He was vomiting. He retreated to the rear. And as the Union troops retreated from that clearing near Chancellorsville, Lee's army had fought itself together, and Lee rode into the middle of his troops. And there was this amazing moment when this spontaneous outpouring of emotion on the part of the Confederates, that's the moment when Lee and his men finished this period of bonding this year that was unmatched in the Civil War. See, there's no way Lee should've won this battle. There's one more day of action a little farther to the east. But in the end, Hooker retreats. He never should've retreated. He was in an impregnable position, but he did retreat. And Lincoln was absolutely beside himself after this. He just couldn't ... Everybody knew what the numbers were. The newspapers had talked about it- ... that Lee had only half as many men as Hooker, and once again, the Army of the Potomac, the largest and most important army of the Republic, has been defeated by this smaller army. It, Lee's sort of legend in the North grew and in the South. He became, by this point, he and his army were the most important national institution in the Confederacy. People looked to them to see whether indep- It's like Washington and the Continental Army during the Revolution. If they're still in the field, there's still a chance for victory. This cemented that position for Lee, this victory at Chancellorsville did, in the minds of Confederates, and made him a kind of bugaboo to people in the North. They were just thirsty for someone to defeat Lee and capture Richmond. - So this, in some sense, created the legend of Robert E. Lee. - It certainly helped solidi- Yes, it did. It went a long way toward doing it. A long way. - So you write about, you know, the difference between sort of reality and memory. How does the North remember this battle, and how does the South remember this battle? - It's really fascinating. The North remembers this battle by not remembering it very much. - Yeah, ignoring it. - They sort of airbrush it out of their memory of the war. The Confederates, in the iconography of the Lost Cause, this ... Lee and Jackson had their last meeting ever here just before the fighting on May 2nd got going, and there was a famous painting of that done by an artist named Julio that was then reprinted as a lithograph that hung in innumerable homes and offices and courthouses in the South. It's Lee and Jackson at high tide, kind of. Gettysburg hasn't happened, never mind Appomattox. These are the two greatest Confederate soldiers at their greatest moment of success. It became hugely important in the Lost Cause telling of the war. On the Union side, they didn't wanna talk about Joseph Hooker that much. They had... They'd rather talk about other things. - Yeah, it's probably one of the most humiliating battles of the war from the Union side. - It, I think it's, it's really, it's just a, it's amazing that Hooker lost this. It's just amazing. And it shows the complete dominance of one personality over another personality, in my view. - So Stonewall Jackson was shot, killed. - Shot by his own men, out trying to reconnoiter and keep the battle going and exploit his successes, carried back to the rear, and he died on May 10th, died eight days later. - So what impact did that have of Stonewall Jackson's death? - Well, that had a hu-- That, there was unbelievable mourning across the Confederacy about that, and even since, really interesting, even some positive comments in the North about how he'd been a sor-- He was misguided, but a very religious guy and all of this stuff, but they're quietly very, "That's really good news for the United States that Stonewall Jackson is dead, and really bad news for the Confederacy." - Outside the myth, did it actually have a practical impact on, on the war? - I don't think so, and the people who love Stonewall Jackson would disagree with me, but I don't see where he would've ... He was a very good soldier at what he did, and Lee used him very well, and they were a good partnership, but I don't see how he would've changed the larger contours of the war. I don't. - If we zoom out and look at Robert E. Lee, somebody you've written about quite a bit, studied a lot, do you think we can use this battle to try to understand the military genius of the man and, in general, who he was? - I do, and it shows both why he was successful and why some of the reasons he was successful opened the way for what should've been big defeats but didn't. I mean, Lee's personality was, at heart, aggressive. His first impulse was always to take the war to the opponent. He said, "They outnumber us. If we just sit and wait for them to come to us, they're gonna have all the advantages. We need to try to disrupt them and look for openings." What this campaign showed was his audacity. He divided his army three times in the course of this campaign in the face of a much more powerful opponent, which showed his audacity. It also highlighted the overall culture that he created in his army, which was a culture of risk-taking, of seeking to inflict the greatest possible harm on your opponent. It's the antithesis of the culture that McClellan created in the Army of the Potomac, which is a culture of caution, of not taking risks, of not doing anything until everything is just right. Any adult knows everything is never just right, so if you're waiting for that, you'll never do anything. It's the, two cultures are absolutely antithetical to one another, and in the end, it shows Lee and how what he had accomplished, he had created an army that was willing to absorb casualties because it won all the time. And they realized that that was, they believed, making it more likely that their whole war effort would be successful. There are only a few times during the war where you get a scene like you got on May 3rd, where this whole army sees the old man ride into their midst, basically, and just has this ... I think they decided at that point, the soldiers, that he was always gonna win, and Lee looked at them and thought, "They can do whatever I ask them to do." I think if you wanna understand Gettysburg, if you wanna understand Pickett's Charge, you need to look back to May 3rd at Chancellorsville, when Lee just decided that his infantry could do anything he wanted them to do. - But also from the infantry perspective, they believed in the- - You asked me earlier about what did the soldiers' letters say. The letters from Lee's army, they absolutely didn't even contemplate losing to the Army of the Potomac. I mean, they just didn't think- They didn't think they would lose to it - What do you attribute that to? Is that, does it, Robert E. Lee, to him? - It's to Lee and the fact that they won these victories under Lee, and that they took these chances, and everybody tried. And they always knew that they were outnumbered, and yet they were still winning. The closest the numbers had ever been at the seven days when the armies were about the same size, but after that, Lee is always at a significant disadvantage in numbers, and yet he seems to be victorious. - So Lee's aggressiveness, like you've mentioned, produced also staggering casualties. - Staggering casualties. He lost 13,000 men here, and Hooker about 17,500. A much higher proportion of Lee's army than Hooker lost in his army. But this should've been a disaster for Lee. Hooker should have crushed Lee here. Absolutely should have crushed Lee, but he didn't. - So there's two cases: Lee's audacity being the South's best hope of winning the war, but the other case is he was actually bleeding the South dry. - Yes, and historians have criticized him for not just being on the defensive all the time. I think Lee understood better than many of his critics now understand that the key was Northern civilian opinion. He said it more than once, "If we win victories, it will depress their morale. If their morale is depressed, the Democrats will do better. If the Democrats get into office, it's good for the Confederacy." And he also knew that he was ... It's a race between, "Am I gonna run out of men before they run out of morale ... in the United States?" I think he understood that, and I think that was the best chance for the Confederacy to win. And in the end, I'm very happy to report, the Confederacy ran out of men before the Union ran out of morale. And so the war went the way it did. But I think Lee was very perceptive in that regard. He understood how important politically what happened militarily was. Much better understanding of that than a lot of people had at the time, and better understanding, I think, than a lot of historians have now. And this is a horrible time for the US because behind the lines, people are in ra- Democrats are unhappy with the Emancipation Proclamation. Just two months before this, Congress passed the Conscription Act. Democrats are very unhappy about that. They're saying that Lincoln is a tyrant. He's forcing people into a war that's not the war they wanted to fight anyway. Union morale is very fragile. Morale, civilian morale at this point, and this makes it much, much worse. The draft riots in New York City, the first draft numbers were pulled in New York City in July. The draft riots come right after Gettysburg, but that is symptomatic of what morale ... Desertions went up in the Army of the Potomac after the Emancipation Proclamation. - So at this point, the Confederacy is arguably very close to winning the war. - I think this is one of the more optimistic points for the Confederacy, is in the late spring and early summer of 1863. Yes, I do. - If Robert E. Lee is correct, in that it's all about morale, which seems like a, a valid argument, then this feels, like, very close to breaking the morale of the Union. - In the Eastern Theater, I think it is, but in the Western Theater we have our boy Grant ... who's operating against Vicksburg at this point. So there are two big campaigns kind of going on at this time, and Vicksburg is the other one. - Can you speak to Vicksburg? This is '63. - Yeah, this is '63, and Vicksburg is the last major Confederate citadel on the Mississippi River. They've already lost New Orleans. They've lost ... So they've lost the river. It's not a Confederate river anymore. But they still have a strong point at Vicksburg, and another one at Port Hudson in Northern Louisiana. Grant has been operating against Vicksburg since the winter of '62, and he's finally, through a series of trial and errors and failures, he's finally found a way that he thinks he can get to the city. He takes great risks. He crosses the Mississippi River after having the Union Navy run past all the batteries, the artillery batteries there at Vicksburg, and he invests the city from the east. He's laying siege to Vicksburg while he's just getting his campaign to do that started when Hooker is at Chancellorsville. In May, he invests the city and begins a siege that will end just as the Battle of Gettysburg ends, and it's, it's one of the most impressive campaigns in US military history, Grant's campaign against Vicksburg. Cuts loose from his supply lines. Nobody understands what he's doing. Sherman doesn't get what he's doing. Lincoln doesn't get what he's doing. And in the end they go, "Oh, that's what you were doing." And it worked. And in the end, he captures Vicksburg, which surrenders on July 4th, 1863. And if you don't think that a kind of religious people didn't read divine intervention into catching, having that happen on July 4th, 1863, you would be incorrect. That's the same day that Lee retreated from Gettysburg. What? Really? God's not putting a thumb on the scales here? Huge victories in the West, huge victory in the East on the anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. - Well, that takes us to Gettysburg. - Here we are at Gettysburg. - Here we go. - Which everybody knows, Lex, is the turning point of the Civil War. - Or is it? Okay. - No. - All right. - Short answer. - Well, that's first ... Before we before we analyze the, its role as a turning point or not- - Yes, yes. - ... what is Gettysburg? July 1863. - Okay. - Walk me through the three days of Gettysburg. - So Joe Hooker retreats across the Rappahannock. Lee is frustrated because he hasn't dealt more damage to Hooker, and this is what he decides to do. He decides to move north for a second time. His army is strengthened. He builds it up to 75,000. This is his army at its absolute apogee as he gets ready to go north. It's confident. It's well-supplied, well-led. And so they head north second week in June, and here's what his goal is. He has two main goals. He wants to take the war out of Virginia so that the agricultural sector isn't subject to the presence of the army, so to let agriculture recover a little, and he wants to provision his army off the rich Cumberland Valley in Pennsylvania, siphon fodder and food and animals while he's north of the Potomac, and he wants to stay up there for a long time to keep the war out of Virginia. He doesn't wanna-- He has no... The movie Gettysburg, he says he wants to capture Washington. No, he doesn't wanna capture Washington. He knows it's too strong. He has no idea of doing that, but he knows he'll pull the Union Army after him and simply reorient the war, and he knows it'll be bad politically for Lincoln- ... if he's actually operating in the United States. So off he goes to the north. He gets north of the river. His cavalry under Jeb Stuart is not doing its job because poor Jeb, who is a very good cavalryman but has a sort of adolescent streak where he has to be praised all the time, he fights a, the biggest cavalry battle of the war near Culpeper, Virginia, Battle of Brandy Station on June the 9th, and he almost loses, and it hurts his little feelings. And so he decides that he needs to do something dramatic so the newspapers will love him again. And he decides to ride all the way around the Army of the Potomac, which he did when McClellan was in command. It's easier to do it when McClellan's in command 'cause he's never moving. He decides he'll do it again here. And just as he gets east of the Army of the Potomac, the Army of the Potomac starts to move north, and so Stuart is trapped with... and he can't communicate with Lee. So Lee doesn't know what's going on 'cause his cavalry isn't doing its job. He spreads his army across southern Pennsylvania and then finds out from a sort of civilian spy, guy named Harrison, that the Army of the Potomac is actually following him and is much closer, and Lee at the end of June orders his army to concentrate near Gettysburg and not to bring on a battle, and they concentrate. Most of them come together. There's a little clash on June the 30th, but on July the 1st, the armies make contact to the west of Gettysburg in a meeting engagement and more troops coming on each side. It builds into what turns into the three-day biggest battle of the Civil War. It's not something Lee had planned, And it wouldn't have happened if his cavalry had been doing its job, but they weren't, and so here they come and there's a battle that goes for three days. Lee has the-- He takes the tactical aggressive every day. He does the attacking. The Federals do the defending. Lee's army's 75,000. The other army's about 85,000, 88,000. And famous terrain, Little Round Top, Round Top, Devil's Den, the Peach Orchard, all these famous places, and it ends on the third day. Lee comes close on the second day, a huge victory for the Confederates on the first day. Third day, Lee's frustrated and he just decides to let his infantry take care of it for him and the result is what most people call Pickett's Charge. Pickett was just a part of the charge. 12 and a half thousand infantry in a direct assault and it fails completely and he retreats the next day. I think you can draw a straight line between May the 3rd at Chancellorsville when his infantry fought their way together and July the 3rd at Gettysburg. He admits it too as he writes letters to both his wife and Jefferson Davis saying, "I asked too much of my infantry. No fault is on them. All the fault is on me." And he was right. All the fault was on him. He and Grant are alike that way. They accept responsibility, not like McClellan. His first reaction is, "It's not my fault," to pick a general at random who did this. "It's not my fault. It must be somebody else's fault." Lee took responsibility. He expected too much from his infantry. His subordinates had not been doing that good a job and they lost the biggest battle of the war. - What was the military mistake there? What could Robert E. Lee have done differently? - I think what he could have done, the most perceptive Confederate soldier who wrote about the war was a guy named Edward Porter Alexander who was the most gifted artillerist. He's in Lee's army. He wrote after the war, Lee won a great victory on July 1st at Gettysburg, smashed two Union infantry corps, had a very strong position. He should've just hunkered down and said, "Okay, attack me. See what you can do." He didn't do that. He almost certainly would've won the battle if he had done that, but he, his, this is where his aggressiveness gets him in trouble. He was pushing for a more aggressive, more decisive outcome right then and he ended up costing... He lost probably 25,000 men at Gettysburg, at least a third of his army. More than that, he went across the river, went across the Potomac with 52 generals in his army. 17 of them became casualties. He lost a third of his entire corps of generals killed, wounded, or captured in the Gettysburg Campaign. It's a really bloody, costly campaign for him and he ends up retreating back into Virginia. It comes to it, and Lincoln is at first very happy about it. There's another, yet another general in command on the Union side. Hooker's gone. A guy named George Meade is in and Meade does what McClellan did after Antietam. He lets Lee get away, doesn't really harass him, and Lincoln is beside himself with disappointment. He writes a letter to Meade, thanks him for his great victory and then says, "You've let him get away. The war is gonna continue indefinitely," says Lincoln. Then he doesn't send the letter to... He writes it but doesn't send it to Meade, but he gets another guy to tell Meade what's in it, so he- ... a guy named Halleck who's the general in chief at that point. Lincoln certainly did not think Gettysburg was the great turning point of the war. He, he probably thought it should've been, but it wasn't because Lee got away with his army intact. And after the battle, Lee said, "Well, you'll see." He said, "They lost a lot too, and they're gonna be... There's not gonna be another big battle." He said, "They'll be as quiet as a sucking dove- ... for six months." And in fact, it's 10 months before there's another big battle in- ... the Eastern Theater, till Grant gets there. - Yeah, so how does Grant come from the, to change the theater from the Western Theater into the Eastern? - So Gettysburg's a really important victory for the United States. - Yeah, but it's not the turning point. - No, and it's not as important as Vicksburg, because Lee gets away. Grant captured an entire rebel army at Vicksburg. Pemberton's whole army surrendered, and that's the second time Grant had forced an army to surrender. He forced one at Fort Donelson back in February of 1862. His victory is ... There are no equivocations about it. It's a victory. The Mississippi is now all controlled by the United States Navy, but Lee got away, so that puts a little cloud over Gettysburg at the time. Grant wins one more victory in the West after this. He wins the Battle of Chattanooga in late 1863. And that then puts him in position for Lincoln to decide that he not only should be in charge of everything in the West, he should be general-in-chief, and that's what brings Grant to the fore. And in March '64, he's now general-in-chief with the new rank of lieutenant general on his ... He's got three stars on his shoulders now instead of two. - And then that where does that take us? That takes us to '64 with the Overland Campaign. That story plus Atlanta, Sherman's March. - That sets up ... Grant is now planning for how the whole war is gonna go. And he envisions five components. The two most important are he's gonna move against Lee, and his plan is lock up with Lee, inflict the greatest possible damage on Lee, prevent Lee from sending reinforcements anywhere else, and if all goes well, Richmond would fall. But he's not mainly interested in Richmond. He's interested in Lee's army, which is what Lincoln has been trying to get his generals to be interested in the whole time. Destroy Lee's army, and of course Richmond falls. - So how is he thinking about the clash with Lee? Grant versus Lee. - Grant versus Lee is just confront him. And they're still near Fredericksburg, where they, on the Rappahannock River frontier, engaged with him and what they ended up with was a period of six weeks of continuous combat that began with the Battle of the Wilderness on May the 5th and 6th. The old pattern in the Civil War, Lex, was you fight a battle, one side retreats. It might be weeks, might be months before you fight again. What happened here is Lee and Grant fought the Battle of the Wilderness. 12,000 Confederate casualties, 18,000 Union 30,000 casualties at the Wilderness. They march for one day. They start another battle, Spotsylvania Courthouse. 12,000 More Confederate casualties, 18,000 more Union casualties, so now you've had 60,000 casualties in two battles with no interval. That continues through May. Cold Harbor, they end up near Richmond at Cold Harbor in early June. Grant launches frontal assaults there. They come to nothing. His men are, many of them are butchered. The bottom line is that in the six-week campaign, Grant suffers 65,000 casualties, which is as big as Lee's whole army had been. Lee suffers 35,000, which is a higher percentage of his army than Grant lost in, or about the same percentage, actually. But it is a kind of continuous campaign no one had seen before, and it shatters both armies. It eviscerates the officer corps in both armies. armies. A lot of soldiers just break down. We would talk about PTSD now probably. They just hadn't been used to something like this. - And this kind of continuous warfare, that's ... We can attribute that to Grant. - Yes, this is ... And this is where the Grant the Butcher image comes in. - But also probably, as hard as it is to say, it's an act of military genius, right? - Well, it's ... He's doing what he wanted to do. He's bleeding Lee's army and at the same time pushing it back toward Richmond, and what it ends up in is the siege at Petersburg, Virginia, which is just south of Richmond and controls the communications into Richmond, and it's a siege of actually Petersburg and Richmond, and that is the thing that Lee feared the most, and Grant had put him in exactly that position. But the perception behind the lines in the United States is endless casualties. Who's winning? We can't even tell who's winning. We have these casualties, and so Union morale drops to its lowest point of the entire war in July and August 1864. Because while this is going on, Sherman is moving against Atlanta, and he is taking his time, not fighting these big battles, but he's not capturing Atlanta either. The whole summer goes by. Atlanta hasn't fallen. Richmond hasn't fallen. There's an election coming up in the fall in the United States, and Lincoln decides ... The morale gets so bad he calls his cabinet together in late August and makes them sign what's been called the Blind Memorandum, and what the memorandum said is, "We're not gonna be reelected, and we're gonna have to win the war before the Democrats come in, because we know they won't win the war." Lincoln did not think they would win. That's in August. And so I think that United States civilian morale, the lowest point of the war for the United States is in July and August 1864. And if we'd been able to stick our microphones in people's faces and said, "Well, but what about Gettysburg? That was the turning point of the war," they would've said, "What are you talking about?" "That was a year ago. This is now, and we're not winning, and it's not worth it, and we're just about ready." McClellan, incidentally, was the Democratic nominee for president that year, so he's running against Lincoln. - So first of all, if Lincoln didn't win, do you think- - Well, we know it would've been good for the Confederates if Lincoln didn't win, but just, uh ... McClellan still ... It's interesting. McClellan was running kind of against the Democratic platform. What the Democratic platform called for was basically negotiations, an armistice and then negotiations. And many people believed if they ever stop fighting, they're not gonna start fighting again. And so some negotiated end to the war that might even yield a confederacy. McClellan, to his credit, and I hate to give him credit, at least said that he wasn't up for that. He said, "We need to win the war, and then we'll have negotiations." But what's clear is... And it would've been, would've been the end of emancipation. The, 'cause emancipation, what became the 13th Amendment had passed through the Senate in April of '64, but the House voted against it. That doesn't, isn't gonna happen till early '65. - How close was it that Lincoln won/lost? - Well, Lincoln won. Grant didn't reelect Lincoln, 'cause he, Grant against Lee would not reelect Lincoln. But other Grants, other things that Grant, part of his overall plan as general-in-chief, Sherman captured Atlanta- ... in early September. And that just changed everything. - That was the real turning point. - That was a huge military turning point, and then on the heels of that, Philip Sheridan won a series of crushing victories in the Shenandoah Valley, the last of which came just before the election, and it was Sherman, and to a lesser degree Sheridan, that reelected Lincoln, and not just Lincoln, but huge Republican majorities- ... in both the House and the Senate in 1864. - And then the thing that broke the back of Confederacies, Sherman's March, 60,000 men across Georgia to the sea, burning the infrastructure. - Yes, as he said, "I'm gonna go across and make Georgia howl," is how he put it. He added a psychological twist. What Grant envisioned his doing, and Sheridan actually did it in the Shenandoah Valley before Sherman did it in Georgia, is go into an agriculturally productive area, burn the mills, kill the livestock, destroy the crops, lay waste to it so that it can't be a logistical support of the Confederacy anymore. Sheridan did it in the Shenandoah Valley, and then Sherman did it in Georgia. But Sherman said, "But I'm also going to break them psychologically." That's what he said, that, "I'm gonna show them that my army can go wherever it wants to go, whenever it wants to go, and there's nothing Jefferson Davis can do about it." He said, "When they decide that, they'll give up." Didn't exactly work that way, but that's what he-- so he marched first to Savannah, and then the final campaign for Sherman was up through the Carolinas. He went up through South Carolina and into North Carolina. And Grant laid siege to Lee, and the siege lasted nine months, the Siege of Petersburg in Richmond, and finally Grant broke Lee's lines on April 1st, 1865. Lee started a retreat. Grant just gave him no pause, and he ran him to ground at Appomattox after about a week, and Lee surrendered. - What do we know about the relationship between the two men?

[TRUNCATED]

items.title: The Rise and Fall of the Roman Empire and the Byzantine Empire | Lex Fridman Podcast #498
items.transcript_text:
- We're talking about a society that was right in the middle of one of the main corridors of empire building and new religions in the world. This is the most dangerous neighborhood that you can possibly live in. - 26 emperors were murdered in a period of 50 years. - Yes. It's tremendous instability. - Almost all were of these emperors were generals, and almost all were murdered by their men. So civil war was the norm, hyperinflation, economic crash, plus there's a plague. There's just a lot of chaos. - Here's why I don't think the Eastern Roman Empire is a military dictatorship. It, it was just very, very well done. He also had Bulgar allies. So these are the, the Bulgars who had just, you know, crossed the Danube just, like, just a few years earlier actually and settled south of the Danube, you know, where eventually, you know, Bulgaria emerged. So he had Bulgar allies, and he used the, the Greek fire very, very strategically. He used his own fleet. He contained the Arabs to certain places where they kind of starved and wore them down. Yeah, it's just very well done. - From a military perspective. - From a military perspective. - Well, was there, was it the, the walls, the navy, the weather, the diplomacy, just good luck that helped Constantinople hold? - I don't see much role for good luck there. I mean, I think he had it all pretty planned out. It was all of the elements that you mentioned. And yeah, he, he just deployed them very, very astutely and went on to rule after that for another 20-some years, and his son continued. Um, they, they formed a dynasty. It was-- We call it the Isaurian dynasty, though they were not from Isauria. - And then from that, the fascinating thing that we mentioned about religion, there was a whole stretch of time marked by intense internal religious conflicts over iconoclasm. Maybe you can clarify this, but so iconoclasm, of course, is whether sacred images, icons, should be venerated or destroyed. This had major political and theological stakes. The seemingly smallest things can have the biggest of conflicts. - Yeah. You've been in an Orthodox church. Have you seen all the icons and the just painting everywhere? Every space that you can imagine is covered in either icons or images or iconography of saints. All right. That's a result of this. No, that's not what Christian churches used to be like, at least not in Constantinople. But his dynasty basically tried to limit, Or remove images from churches, and ultimately that policy failed. And the other side that wanted images or liked images, or let me put it differently, thought that images were not only appropriate but helpful in the context of Christian worship prevailed. And so gradually the churches began to fill up with icons, lots of icons. They're almost like, you know, like a catchword for Orthodox, you know, devotion. Um, I have icons at home. You have a little corner in the house and you have little iconography. Um, anyway, I mean, as a secular Orthodox person, but I... even I can't get away from them. - But that has serious consequences. I mean, that was- ... serious. It was an extremely serious internal religious conflict. - Well, okay, so one asterisk on that. In my research, I did not find a popular interest in this matter. Like- - Oh, interesting - ... yeah, I don't- - So this is an overblown- - Yes. Yes, socially completely overblown. - Oh, this is one of those things where religious folks will write the story of history. - That's it. Got it. - Ah. - You got it. I could not find... There were, like, a few emperors, and there's some bishops and abbots and monks. Like, I don't know, maybe 100, 200 people are, like, seriously invested in this, and they're going at it. But these are the people who write the texts. But they never mention, for example, that, oh, you know, the people of Constantinople, they rose up, and they demanded icons or not icons or anything like that. Nah, never. So in my view, this is one of those controversies that's only a few people really, really cared- ... about it, and unfortunately, they're the ones who wrote the sources. - So you always have to, Be very careful to consider the sources when you're reading about anything involving religious events. - Or any kind of events. - But certain things are more intensely, People are more intensely passionate about- ... and therefore they're going, that bias is going to- - Yeah, yeah - ... bleed into the way you report the history. - Yeah. And not only that, when emperors changed their policy, almost everyone fell into line. They switched positions. It's like, "No, yeah, whatever. Put the images, take the images," like, whatever. I mean, like this isn't, they did not see this as central. Some people did, and they got very worked up about it. Anyway, but in the end, the pro-icon position won, and their view just began to fill up the space. Like, like it literally was filling up the churches, and it still does. - The thing is, we somehow took on the impossible task of talking about a thousand- - It'll defeat you, man. It'll defeat you every time. - I mean, there's a reason why you really wanna do a thousand-hour podcast on this, right? As, as, as you do, as there's so many incredible conversations about every single emperor, every single nuanced detail of the emperors. It really is a, is a thriving civilization. It's a thriving empire which in it contains so many lessons for even the modern times. But anyway, you have written one of the books is Streams of Gold, Rivers of Blood: The Rise and Fall of Byzantium, 955 AD to the First Crusade. So this period has... We talked about survival and some low points. This is a period where, once again, there's some flourishing. So by the 10th century in the Macedonian era, the empire is back. It's wealthy, it's culturally confident, and under emperors like Basil II, Who I think is in your top 10 list. it is expanding again, and this is a period that you describe in part in your book, Streams of Gold, Rivers of Blood. So how did Byzantium go from surviving to expanding again? - So I wrote that book in part in order to test myself and see if I could write narrative. So I hadn't written a history narrative book up until that point. Everything I wrote was sort of analytical, right? And it was successful enough that a few years later, my editor asked me to write the big history, the new Roman Empire- - Yeah - ... the thousand page- - Of the whole thing - ... of the whole thing. And so I set for myself the task of explaining in this book, Streams of Gold, Rivers of Blood, a very particular period that was marked by a sudden turn to conquest again after a long period of more or less defensive war. 955, there's a new military leadership is appointed, and the Romans go conquering again, especially in Cilicia, northern Syria, and Cyprus, and the Caucasus, and then eventually also Bulgaria. And then right afterwards, they have this generation plus period of stability and prosperity, and then they're hit by a triple whammy. These are three new attackers. So it's primarily the Seljuk Turks coming in from the east, some Pechenegs coming down from the north over the Danube, And the Normans in southern Italy. And under the pressure of this three-part attack, the, you know, this expansionist what had become more imperial state buckles. And enters another one of these crises, just like the one we described for the seventh century. You know, survives it by the skin of its teeth. And goes on again to rebuild and become prosperous, wealthy, and powerful again, as it does throughout its history. It's these cycles. So I just wanted to describe that iteration of that- ... that process, and that's what I do in that book. - So I think the traditional view, In this perfect storm of the 11th century is that it was more to do with the internal sort of moral decay and, Civilian emperors neglecting the army, this internal stuff. And you make the case that it's the external stuff, the three-prong attack, like you said, Normans in the west, the Turkic steppe people in the north, and in Central Asia, the Turks in the east. Can you describe that, the three forces in the case that that was the main reason why it hit a low? - Well, this is also a methodological problem, right? In other words, when you're looking at a society that suddenly faces a bunch of problems, and you could, you know, reasonably make the case for a kind of decline or a crisis, is your instinct, it's your first instinct to suppose that there must be something wrong in the internal mechanisms of that society that, you know, led it to fail, which is what my field has done traditionally. Uh, in part because of the decline and fall model, right, of this society, we're kind of primed to think that there was something wrong with it. It's a long story. Or is it reasonable to say that a society that does not seem to have any, like, particularly serious structural flaws is hit by external, you know, challenges that it couldn't realistically have foreseen or prepared for such that, you know, it, it couldn't cope with them and, as I said, buckled. And I think that's what happened. I think that's the, main narrative. Not that there weren't problems. There were. But no state can, I mean, medieval or ancient, can realistically survive the simultaneous attack of three very different kinds of enemies, the Normans or, like, these knights... Like a new type of Western warfare that is just all about, you know, grinding the enemy to bits. But who are also terrorists. Like, they're straight up terrorists. - Normans are fascinating because, I mean, there's... ... there's a Viking component too- - Yeah, yeah, yeah. - ... with the Normans. - Yeah, yeah. - That's a whole... So they have, they have three different kinds of enemies. - Yes. The Pechenegs, who's, you know, a, a totally different type of, you know, probably mostly nomadic horsemen. And then the Seljuk Turks who are also mostly nomadic horsemen, but who are coming in from Central Asia with vast reserves of manpower behind them. In fact, either intending to or, as it happens, effecting a demographic change in not just demographic, but ecological too, because they basically, when they move into Asia Minor, they're transforming or terraforming, Agricultural land into pasturage. And, and they're just backed by reserves of manpower that no other enemy of the empire has had yet. Uh, so yeah, how do you, how do you cope with these situations? I mean, they're, it's very, very difficult, and it's a wonder that they survived it at all. Now, they also have internal problems, and I'm not gonna sort of try to sweep these under the rug, right? In particular, we're seeing the end of the Macedonian dynasty. This is a dynasty that had lasted for about two centuries, and this has a kind of politically destabilizing effect. New emperors, and there are a lot of, like, childless old men in this period, are relatively insecure. They don't have this sort of a dynastic glitz behind them, and so they're tending to, to buy a lot of political support, like hand out these exemptions, give cash, you know, titles to anyone who will support them, and this, of course, causes a budget problem. Like, they don't have enough money after a while. And then they have to start raising all of these armies to deal with all of these problems, and that just increases the pressure on the budget, and so there is an internal problem as well, yeah. - So you mentioned this loop of thriving and then having to survive, surviving, that happens a few times- ... throughout the history of the Roman Empire. It seems that societies in general oscillate in that way. Is there something particular you could say about the oscillations, the loops that the Roman Empire goes through? - Yes. Now, I don't think this is an oscillation. At least that's not how I think of it in my own mind. Um, so as I explained, the crises that this, this polity, this state, this society that it undergoes are dis- there are a discrete number of them. I can tell you what they are, and we've talked about most of them so far. They don't last very long, and they are all sudden challenges that appear from the outside. In other words, they're exogenous shocks, that they can't really have prepared for. These shocks cause massive territorial loss, which requires adjustment, right? But they don't last that long. In other words, the Romans almost always, at some point, figure out how to hold a line, how to consolidate their position, regroup- and put their economy and their society back on a trajectory of revival, regrowth, and eventual reconquest. Always. Every singl
